summary: 1954 steel fire-spotting tower on Healing Springs Mountain, Davidson County, built by Wagner Construction Co.; no source found on its fate or current site.

facts.design: Steel tower with a glass-enclosed cab
facts.agency: North Carolina Division of Forest Resources

events.note: Built by Wagner Construction Company of Salisbury; blasting hard rock for the foundation made construction take longer than expected
Put into service before construction was finished, during dangerous fire conditions; a man worked in the glass cab with field glasses and a two-way radio

evidence.supports: built by Wagner Construction Company of Salisbury
evidence.quote: The tower was built by Wagner Construction Company, of Salisbury.

evidence.supports: foundation work took much longer because of blasting hard rock
evidence.quote: It took much longer to build than expected, because of the difficulty in blasting hard rock at the base to set up a foundation.

evidence.supports: 73-foot steel tower with a glass-enclosed cab on Healing Springs Mountain
evidence.quote: There's a tiny glass enclosed cubbyhole atop a 73-foot steel tower on Healing Springs mountain.

evidence.supports: first forest fire spotting tower erected in Davidson County
evidence.quote: is the first forest fire spotting tower ever erected in Davidson County.

evidence.supports: placed in service before completion because of dangerous fire conditions
evidence.quote: the tower was placed in service several days ago because of the extremely dangerous fire situation existing in this area

evidence.supports: a man in the cab with field glasses and a two-way radio
evidence.quote: In this cubbyhole there is a man, armed with field glasses and a two-way radio

evidence.supports: fire spotting for two years had been done from the city's big water tank
evidence.quote: For the past two years much of the fire spotting in this area has been done from atop the city's big water tank, where a telephone has been installed.

evidence.supports: site on property of the J.M. Daniel estate, leased with the road and a power line
evidence.quote: It is located on property belonging to J.M. Daniel estate. The property has been leased, along with property over which the road winds, as well as that covered by a power line leading to the tower.

evidence.supports: the index lists the North Carolina Division of Forest Resources as agency
evidence.quote: HIGH ROCK Davidson County - North Carolina Division of Forest Resources

evidence.supports: tower work started about five weeks before the October 1954 report, and was not yet complete when placed in service (supports 1954 build and service before completion)
evidence.quote: Work on the structure started over five weeks ago, but still isn't quite complete.

evidence.supports: date of the newspaper report quoted by the index

sources.title: North Carolina lookouts index, High Rock entry (quoting The Dispatch, October 12, 1954)

notes_for_editor: Only one source was read: the Forest Lookouts North Carolina index, which reprints an October 12, 1954 item from The Dispatch. The original newspaper was not checked. No source found gives the tower's removal date or current condition, so the story says no source describes the site today. Search results for High Rock mostly returned other towers (Washington, Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania) and High Rock Lake; none of those is this tower. The 1954 text places the tower on Healing Springs Mountain, but the record's coordinates (35.62472, -80.19) sit near High Rock Lake, so the location should be checked. A search snippet, not read, described a gated subdivision on High Rock Mountain; it is an unverified lead, not used in the story.
